claim: Chromosome scattering volume (CSV) is reduced soon after nuclear envelope breakdown (NEBD) in human cells.
source: Here, we quantify chromosome-scattering volume (CSV) and find that it is reduced soon after nuclear envelope breakdown (NEBD) in human cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B demonstrating CSV reduction after NEBD.

claim: CSV reduction occurs primarily independently of microtubules.
source: The CSV reduction occurs primarily independently of microtubules and is therefore not an outcome of interactions between chromosomes and the spindle.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1C showing CSV reduction in nocodazole-treated cells lacking microtubules.

claim: An acto-myosin network is assembled on the cytoplasmic surface of the nuclear envelope prior to NEBD in a LINC complex-dependent manner.
source: We find that, prior to NEBD, an acto-myosin network is assembled in a LINC complex-dependent manner on the cytoplasmic surface of the nuclear envelope.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figures 2A, 2B, and 2C showing actin accumulation on the NE and its dependence on LINC complex.

claim: The acto-myosin network remains on nuclear envelope remnants soon after NEBD.
source: This acto-myosin network remains on nuclear envelope remnants soon after NEBD, and its myosin-II-mediated contraction reduces CSV and facilitates timely chromosome congression and correct segregation.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2 showing persistence of actin network after NEBD.

claim: Myosin-II-mediated contraction of the acto-myosin network reduces CSV.
source: This acto-myosin network remains on nuclear envelope remnants soon after NEBD, and its myosin-II-mediated contraction reduces CSV and facilitates timely chromosome congression and correct segregation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3A showing that myosin II inhibition with pnBB alleviates CSV reduction.

claim: Myosin-II-mediated contraction of the acto-myosin network facilitates timely chromosome congression.
source: This acto-myosin network remains on nuclear envelope remnants soon after NEBD, and its myosin-II-mediated contraction reduces CSV and facilitates timely chromosome congression and correct segregation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B showing delayed congression when the network is disrupted.

claim: Myosin-II-mediated contraction of the acto-myosin network facilitates correct chromosome segregation.
source: This acto-myosin network remains on nuclear envelope remnants soon after NEBD, and its myosin-II-mediated contraction reduces CSV and facilitates timely chromosome congression and correct segregation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5E showing increased abnormal chromosome segregation when the network is disrupted.

claim: Chromosomes must be efficiently captured by spindle microtubules during mitosis to ensure proper segregation.
source: To ensure proper segregation during mitosis, chromosomes must be efficiently captured by spindle microtubules and subsequently aligned on the mitotic spindle.
evidence: Based on established understanding of mitotic processes and cited literature.

claim: The efficacy of chromosome interaction with the spindle can be influenced by how widely chromosomes are scattered in space.
source: The efficacy of chromosome interaction with the spindle can be influenced by how widely chromosomes are scattered in space.
evidence: Based on logical reasoning about spatial relationships between chromosomes and spindle.

claim: CSV was prominently reduced within the first 8 min following NEBD.
source: We found that CSV was prominently reduced within the first 8 min following NEBD, and reduction continued more slowly over the following ~10 min (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1B graphs.

claim: CSV reduction continued more slowly over approximately 10 minutes after the initial 8 minutes following NEBD.
source: We found that CSV was prominently reduced within the first 8 min following NEBD, and reduction continued more slowly over the following ~10 min (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1B graphs.

claim: CSV reduction was also observed in asynchronous, wild-type U2OS cells.
source: CSV reduction was also observed in asynchronous, wild-type U2OS cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that it was not an artifact caused by cdk1-as-mediated cell cycle synchronization.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: CSV reduction is not an artifact caused by cdk1-as-mediated cell cycle synchronization.
source: CSV reduction was also observed in asynchronous, wild-type U2OS cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that it was not an artifact caused by cdk1-as-mediated cell cycle synchronization.
evidence: Inferred from observation that CSV reduction occurs in both synchronized cdk1-as cells and asynchronous wild-type cells.

claim: After nocodazole treatment, microtubules were almost completely depleted.
source: After nocodazole treatment, MTs were almost completely depleted (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: In control cells, chromosomes moved inward after NEBD and subsequently aligned on the metaphase plate.
source: In control cells, chromosomes moved inward after NEBD, and subsequently aligned on the metaphase plate (Figure 1C, top-row images; Video 1).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1C and Video 1.

claim: In cells lacking visible microtubules, chromosomes moved inward after NEBD but then remained in a spherical formation.
source: In cells lacking visible MTs, chromosomes also moved inward after NEBD, but then remained in a spherical formation (Figure 1C, bottom-row images; Video 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1C, Video 1, and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: CSV was reduced with very similar kinetics in both the presence and absence of microtubules.
source: The CSV was reduced with very similar kinetics in both the presence and absence of MTs (Figure 1C, graphs).
evidence: Supported by quantitative comparison shown in Figure 1C graphs.

claim: The overall CSV reduction observed following NEBD is not an outcome of chromosome interaction with spindle microtubules.
source: Consequently, we conclude that the overall CSV reduction observed following NEBD is not an outcome of chromosome interaction with spindle MTs.
evidence: Inferred from data showing CSV reduction occurs similarly with and without microtubules.

claim: CSV may be slightly smaller at 4 min following NEBD in control cells compared to nocodazole-treated cells.
source: CSV may be slightly smaller at 4 min following NEBD in control cells; if so, this could be due to mild compression of the nuclear envelope (NE) remnants caused by the rapid MT-dependent inward movement of centrosomes (Figure 1C, image at +4 min in control).
evidence: Based on observation of data in Figure 1C and reasoning about centrosome movement.

claim: Mild compression of nuclear envelope remnants at 4 min after NEBD in control cells could be due to rapid MT-dependent inward movement of centrosomes.
source: CSV may be slightly smaller at 4 min following NEBD in control cells; if so, this could be due to mild compression of the nuclear envelope (NE) remnants caused by the rapid MT-dependent inward movement of centrosomes (Figure 1C, image at +4 min in control).
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed difference in CSV at 4 min.

claim: Chromosome mass volume (CMV) did not considerably change following NEBD.
source: Unlike the CSV, the CMV did not considerably change following NEBD.
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The reduction in CSV was not due to chromosome condensation.
source: Thus, we conclude that the reduction in CSV was not due to chromosome condensation, which likely occurs mainly before NEBD (Mora-Bermúdez et al., 2007).
evidence: Inferred from CMV data and cited literature on timing of chromosome condensation.

claim: Chromosome condensation likely occurs mainly before NEBD.
source: Thus, we conclude that the reduction in CSV was not due to chromosome condensation, which likely occurs mainly before NEBD (Mora-Bermúdez et al., 2007).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: In early mitosis, an actin network accumulated on the nuclear envelope, peaking in intensity around NEBD and persisting after it.
source: Consistent with this model, we found that in early mitosis an actin network accumulated on the NE, peaking in intensity around NEBD and persisting after it (Figure 2A; Video 2).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2A and Video 2.

claim: The volume inside the actin network was rapidly reduced within 6 min following NEBD.
source: The volume inside this actin network was rapidly reduced within 6 min following NEBD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting the contraction of the network.
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The rapid reduction in volume inside the actin network within 6 min following NEBD suggests contraction of the network.
source: The volume inside this actin network was rapidly reduced within 6 min following NEBD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting the contraction of the network.
evidence: Inferred from volume measurements.

claim: During the first 6 minutes after NEBD, chromosomes were surrounded by the actin network.
source: During this time, the chromosomes were surrounded by, and the outermost chromosomes were found immediately adjacent to, the actin network (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Video 3).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Video 3.

claim: The outermost chromosomes were found immediately adjacent to the actin network during the first 6 minutes after NEBD.
source: During this time, the chromosomes were surrounded by, and the outermost chromosomes were found immediately adjacent to, the actin network (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Video 3).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Video 3.

claim: The actin network was also observed in wild-type U2OS cells.
source: We used cdk1-as in these experiments to synchronize cells, however the actin network was also observed in wild-type U2OS cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, yellow arrowheads), indicating that it is not an artifact due to cdk1-as regulation.
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The actin network is not an artifact due to cdk1-as regulation.
source: We used cdk1-as in these experiments to synchronize cells, however the actin network was also observed in wild-type U2OS cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, yellow arrowheads), indicating that it is not an artifact due to cdk1-as regulation.
evidence: Inferred from observation in both cdk1-as and wild-type cells.

claim: The actin network was separated outwardly from lamin B1 by 150–200 nm.
source: The actin network was separated outwardly from lamin B1 by 150–200 nm (Figure 2B), suggesting that it may localize on the cytoplasmic surface of the NE (or its remnants) following NEBD.
evidence: Supported by super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The actin network may localize on the cytoplasmic surface of the nuclear envelope or its remnants following NEBD.
source: The actin network was separated outwardly from lamin B1 by 150–200 nm (Figure 2B), suggesting that it may localize on the cytoplasmic surface of the NE (or its remnants) following NEBD.
evidence: Inferred from spatial separation data and knowledge of lamin B1 localization.

claim: Lamin B1 is found on the nucleoplasmic surface of the nuclear envelope.
source: Using Airyscan super-resolution microscopy, we compared the localization of the actin network and the lamin B1 network; the latter is found on the nucleoplasmic surface of the NE (Ungricht and Kutay, 2017) and remains substantially intact soon after NEBD (Georgatos et al., 1997).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: Lamin B1 remains substantially intact soon after NEBD.
source: Using Airyscan super-resolution microscopy, we compared the localization of the actin network and the lamin B1 network; the latter is found on the nucleoplasmic surface of the NE (Ungricht and Kutay, 2017) and remains substantially intact soon after NEBD (Georgatos et al., 1997).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: The LINC complex is a candidate receptor for the actin network on the nuclear envelope.
source: A candidate receptor for the actin network on the NE is the LINC (linker of nucleoskeleton and cytoskeleton) complex, one end of which is anchored in the NE while the other end extends to the cytoplasm and interacts with actin (Luxton and Starr, 2014).
evidence: Based on known properties of the LINC complex from cited literature.

claim: One end of the LINC complex is anchored in the nuclear envelope while the other end extends to the cytoplasm and interacts with actin.
source: A candidate receptor for the actin network on the NE is the LINC (linker of nucleoskeleton and cytoskeleton) complex, one end of which is anchored in the NE while the other end extends to the cytoplasm and interacts with actin (Luxton and Starr, 2014).
evidence: Based on cited literature describing LINC complex structure and function.

claim: The fluorescence intensity of the actin network was significantly diminished in cells expressing LINC-DN compared with cells expressing its control.
source: Crucially, the fluorescence intensity of the actin network was significantly diminished in cells expressing LINC-DN, compared with cells expressing its control (Figure 2C, magenta arrowheads, graph).
evidence: Supported by quantitative fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The actin network localizes to the cytoplasmic surface of the nuclear envelope and its remnants following NEBD in a LINC complex-dependent manner.
source: Therefore, the actin network localizes to the cytoplasmic surface of the NE and its remnants, following NEBD, in a LINC complex-dependent manner.
evidence: Inferred from LINC-DN experiments and spatial localization data.

claim: CSV reduction was incomplete after NEBD with LINC-DN expression compared with control expression.
source: We tested this hypothesis by measuring the CSV in cells expressing LINC-DN and its control (Figure 2D; Video 4) and found that the CSV reduction was incomplete after NEBD with the LINC-DN expression, compared with the control expression.
evidence: Supported by quantitative CSV measurements shown in Figure 2D.

claim: It is likely that the actin network on nuclear envelope remnants confines chromosomes and its contraction leads to CSV reduction.
source: Thus, it is likely that the actin network on NE remnants confines chromosomes and that its contraction leads to CSV reduction.
evidence: Inferred from LINC-DN experiments showing incomplete CSV reduction when actin network is disrupted.

claim: Jasplakinolide, an actin depolymerization inhibitor, had no effect on CSV reduction after NEBD.
source: An actin depolymerization inhibitor jasplakinolide had no effect on CSV reduction after NEBD (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), although it successfully inhibited subsequent cytokinesis as previously reported (Murthy and Wadsworth, 2005).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Jasplakinolide successfully inhibited cytokinesis.
source: An actin depolymerization inhibitor jasplakinolide had no effect on CSV reduction after NEBD (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), although it successfully inhibited subsequent cytokinesis as previously reported (Murthy and Wadsworth, 2005).
evidence: Based on experimental observation and cited literature.

claim: It is unlikely that actin depolymerization promotes actin network contraction or CSV reduction.
source: Thus it is unlikely that actin depolymerization promotes actin network contraction or CSV reduction.
evidence: Inferred from jasplakinolide experiment showing no effect on CSV reduction.

claim: Myosin II is a major mediator of acto-myosin contractility in non-muscle cells.
source: The actin-dependent motor protein myosin II is a major mediator of acto-myosin contractility in non-muscle cells (Svitkina, 2018).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: Myosin II co-localized with the actin network on the nuclear envelope.
source: We found that myosin II co-localized with the actin network on the NE (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, yellow arrowheads).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: pnBB treatment alleviated both CSV reduction and actin network contraction following NEBD.
source: Notably, pnBB treatment alleviated both the CSV reduction (Figure 3A; Video 5) and the actin network contraction (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B) following NEBD, which suggests that these processes are dependent on the myosin II activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: CSV reduction and actin network contraction following NEBD are dependent on myosin II activity.
source: Notably, pnBB treatment alleviated both the CSV reduction (Figure 3A; Video 5) and the actin network contraction (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B) following NEBD, which suggests that these processes are dependent on the myosin II activity.
evidence: Inferred from pnBB inhibition experiments.

claim: pnBB treatment did not affect chromosome mass volume (CMV) after NEBD.
source: On the other hand, the pnBB treatment did not affect CMV (see Figure 1—figure supplement 5) after NEBD (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: While myosin II activity facilitates CSV reduction, this reduction is not due to enhanced chromosome condensation.
source: This suggests that, while myosin II activity facilitates CSV reduction, this reduction is not due to enhanced chromosome condensation.
evidence: Inferred from CMV data showing no change with pnBB treatment.

claim: pnBB treatment did not significantly change the distance between spindle poles soon after NEBD.
source: Moreover, pnBB treatment did not significantly change the distance between spindle poles soon after NEBD (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: pnBB-treated cells did not seem to show considerably altered shapes of the spindle compared with control cells following NEBD.
source: As far as we observed, pnBB-treated cells did not seem to show considerably altered shapes of the spindle (Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 5), compared with control (and LINC-DN-expressing) cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 6), following NEBD.
evidence: Based on qualitative assessment of imaging data.

claim: It seems unlikely that the alleviated CSV reduction due to pnBB treatment was the outcome of an abnormal mitotic spindle.
source: Thus, it seems unlikely that the alleviated CSV reduction due to pnBB treatment was the outcome of an abnormal mitotic spindle.
evidence: Inferred from observations of spindle morphology and pole distance.

claim: pnBB treatment often caused the actin network to extend beyond the spindle poles at the initiation of spindle formation.
source: Nonetheless, pnBB treatment often caused the actin network to extend beyond the spindle poles at the initiation of spindle formation (Figure 3—figure supplement 5, pnBB, 5–20 min).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: pnBB treatment alleviated CSV reduction in the presence of nocodazole.
source: Furthermore, the pnBB treatment alleviated the CSV reduction in the presence of nocodazole (Figure 3B; Video 6), indicating that myosin II promotes actin network contraction and CSV reduction after NEBD in a spindle MT-independent manner.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Myosin II promotes actin network contraction and CSV reduction after NEBD in a spindle MT-independent manner.
source: Furthermore, the pnBB treatment alleviated the CSV reduction in the presence of nocodazole (Figure 3B; Video 6), indicating that myosin II promotes actin network contraction and CSV reduction after NEBD in a spindle MT-independent manner.
evidence: Inferred from experiments combining pnBB and nocodazole treatments.

claim: Double treatment with pnBB and nocodazole seemed to further alleviate CSV reduction during 0–6 min compared with pnBB treatment alone.
source: Double treatment with pnBB and nocodazole seemed to further alleviate the CSV reduction during 0–6 min, compared with pnBB treatment alone (compare Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Based on comparison of data in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: A MT-dependent mechanism and a myosin II-dependent mechanism may work in concert to reduce CSV during 0-6 minutes after NEBD.
source: Thus, a MT-dependent mechanism, leading to mild NE remnant compression by centrosomes (see Figure 1C), and a myosin II-dependent mechanism may work in concert to reduce CSV during this period.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of single and double treatment effects.

claim: In the exposed half of the nucleus treated with azBB, CSV reduction was alleviated compared to the non-exposed half.
source: In the exposed half of the nucleus (Figure 4B,C; blue), the CSV reduction was alleviated, compared to the non-exposed half (red).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In cells not treated with azBB (control), there was no significant difference in CSV between exposed and non-exposed halves of nuclei.
source: In the cells not treated with azBB (control), there was no significant difference in CSV between exposed (Figure 4B,C; green) and non-exposed (orange) halves of nuclei.
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Myosin II activity within the actin network on nuclear envelope remnants causes its contraction and CSV reduction after NEBD.
source: These results support a model in which myosin II activity within the actin network (hereafter referred to as the 'acto-myosin' network) on NE remnants causes its contraction and CSV reduction after NEBD.
evidence: Inferred from azBB photoactivation experiments and other myosin II inhibition data.

claim: LINC-DN expression led to a considerable delay in chromosome congression compared with the control.
source: LINC-DN expression led to a considerable delay in chromosome congression and anaphase onset, compared with the control (Figure 5A–C; Video 7), which was not associated with significant defects in spindle positioning or length (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative timing measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claim: LINC-DN expression led to a considerable delay in anaphase onset compared with the control.
source: LINC-DN expression led to a considerable delay in chromosome congression and anaphase onset, compared with the control (Figure 5A–C; Video 7), which was not associated with significant defects in spindle positioning or length (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative timing measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The delay in chromosome congression and anaphase onset with LINC-DN expression was not associated with significant defects in spindle positioning or length.
source: LINC-DN expression led to a considerable delay in chromosome congression and anaphase onset, compared with the control (Figure 5A–C; Video 7), which was not associated with significant defects in spindle positioning or length (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In cells expressing LINC-DN, chromosomes often remained behind a spindle pole and outside of the pole-to-pole region after NEBD (back-of-spindle chromosomes).
source: In cells expressing LINC-DN, chromosomes often remained behind a spindle pole and outside of the pole-to-pole region after NEBD (back-of-spindle chromosomes) (Figure 5A bottom and D, magenta arrowheads), which is consistent with the extension of NE remnants beyond spindle poles when contraction of the acto-myosin network was suppressed (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5A and quantified in Figure 5D.

claim: The occurrence of back-of-spindle chromosomes in LINC-DN expressing cells is consistent with the extension of nuclear envelope remnants beyond spindle poles when contraction of the acto-myosin network was suppressed.
source: In cells expressing LINC-DN, chromosomes often remained behind a spindle pole and outside of the pole-to-pole region after NEBD (back-of-spindle chromosomes) (Figure 5A bottom and D, magenta arrowheads), which is consistent with the extension of NE remnants beyond spindle poles when contraction of the acto-myosin network was suppressed (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of LINC-DN and pnBB effects.

claim: In a subgroup of cells expressing LINC-DN where back-of-spindle chromosomes still remained at 20 min after NEBD, there was a larger delay in congression.
source: In a subgroup of cells expressing LINC-DN where back-of-spindle chromosomes still remained at 20 min after NEBD in cells, there was a larger delay in congression (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: LINC-DN expression led to more frequent abnormal segregation of chromosomes during anaphase.
source: Moreover, LINC-DN expression led to more frequent abnormal segregation of chromosomes during anaphase (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The results with LINC-DN expression were reproduced with pnBB treatment (which inhibits myosin II).
source: The above results with LINC-DN expression were reproduced with pnBB treatment (which inhibits myosin II) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: CSV reduction due to contraction of the acto-myosin network diminishes back-of-spindle chromosomes and facilitates correct chromosome interaction with spindle microtubules.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that the CSV reduction due to contraction of the acto-myosin network diminishes back-of-spindle chromosomes and facilitates correct chromosome interaction with spindle MTs.
evidence: Inferred from LINC-DN and pnBB experiments showing increased back-of-spindle chromosomes and delayed congression.

claim: CSV reduction due to contraction of the acto-myosin network leads to timely chromosome congression and anaphase onset as well as high-fidelity chromosome segregation.
source: These effects likely lead to timely chromosome congression and anaphase onset as well as high-fidelity chromosome segregation.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing delays and errors when the mechanism is disrupted.

claim: RPE cells showed accumulation of actin on the nuclear envelope in early mitosis.
source: RPE cells (diploid) showed accumulation of actin on the NE in early mitosis (Figure 5—figure supplement 4, top).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: HeLa cells did not show nuclear envelope-associated actin accumulation in early mitosis.
source: By contrast, HeLa cells (highly aneuploid) did not show such NE-associated actin accumulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 4, bottom).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: A lack of the acto-myosin network may be correlated with aneuploidy.
source: An interesting possibility is that a lack of the acto-myosin network is correlated with aneuploidy.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on observation that HeLa cells (aneuploid) lack the network while RPE and U2OS cells have it.

claim: In prophase, the acto-myosin network is formed on the cytoplasmic side of the nuclear envelope, relying on the LINC complex.
source: In prophase, the acto-myosin network is formed on the cytoplasmic side of the NE, relying on the LINC complex.
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple experiments.

claim: Following NEBD, the activity of myosin-II in the acto-myosin network promotes contraction of this network on the nuclear envelope remnants.
source: Following NEBD, the activity of myosin-II in the acto-myosin network promotes contraction of this network on the NE remnants.
evidence: Summary of findings from myosin II inhibition experiments.

claim: Contraction of the acto-myosin network reduces CSV following NEBD, which facilitates chromosome alignment on the metaphase spindle (congression).
source: This contraction reduces CSV following NEBD, which in turn seems to facilitate chromosome alignment on the metaphase spindle (congression) and to ensure high-fidelity chromosome segregation.
evidence: Summary of findings from functional experiments.

claim: Contraction of the acto-myosin network ensures high-fidelity chromosome segregation.
source: This contraction reduces CSV following NEBD, which in turn seems to facilitate chromosome alignment on the metaphase spindle (congression) and to ensure high-fidelity chromosome segregation.
evidence: Summary of findings from functional experiments.

claim: LINC-DN expression and pnBB treatment mainly delayed chromosome movement to the middle of the spindle, rather than the initial interaction.
source: We presume that LINC-DN expression and pnBB treatment mainly delayed chromosome movement to the middle of the spindle, rather than the initial interaction.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on timing of CSV reduction and chromosome movements.

claim: LINC-DN expression and pnBB treatment diminished CSV reduction during 8–16 min after NEBD.
source: Consistent with this notion, LINC-DN expression and pnBB treatment diminished CSV reduction during 8–16 min after NEBD (Figures 2D and 3A); however at this stage, the initial chromosome–MT interaction had likely already occurred – for example, during 6–8 min after NEBD, many chromosomes had moved inward away from the NE remnants, probably due to MT interaction (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: Based on analysis of data in Figures 2D, 3A, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: During 6–8 min after NEBD, many chromosomes had moved inward away from the nuclear envelope remnants, probably due to microtubule interaction.
source: Consistent with this notion, LINC-DN expression and pnBB treatment diminished CSV reduction during 8–16 min after NEBD (Figures 2D and 3A); however at this stage, the initial chromosome–MT interaction had likely already occurred – for example, during 6–8 min after NEBD, many chromosomes had moved inward away from the NE remnants, probably due to MT interaction (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: Based on observation of chromosome movements in imaging data.

claim: The appearance of back-of-spindle chromosomes after LINC-DN expression was well correlated with a delay in chromosome congression.
source: Moreover, the appearance of back-of-spindle chromosomes after LINC-DN expression was well correlated with a delay in chromosome congression (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: During 8–16 min after NEBD, the contractile acto-myosin network constrained chromosomes within the pole-to-pole region, thus reducing the occurrence of back-of-spindle chromosomes and facilitating chromosome movement to the middle of the spindle.
source: We reason that, during 8–16 min after NEBD, the contractile acto-myosin network constrained chromosomes within the pole-to-pole region (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), thus reducing the occurrence of back-of-spindle chromosomes (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 3D) and facilitating chromosome movement to the middle of the spindle, that is congression.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental observations.

claim: CSV reduction also occurs during an earlier phase (0–8 min after NEBD), and it is possible that the earlier CSV reduction facilitates the initial chromosome–MT interaction.
source: However, the CSV reduction also occurs during an earlier phase (0–8 min after NEBD), and it is very possible that the earlier CSV reduction facilitates the initial chromosome–MT interaction.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on timing of CSV reduction.

claim: Contraction of the acto-myosin network on nuclear envelope remnants starts immediately after NEBD to facilitate CSV reduction.
source: Our result suggests that contraction of the acto-myosin network on NE remnants starts immediately after NEBD to facilitate CSV reduction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1B).
evidence: Based on temporal analysis of volume and CSV measurements.

claim: NEBD may reduce tension on the nuclear envelope, which may trigger the contraction of the acto-myosin network on the nuclear envelope remnants.
source: We speculate that NEBD reduces tension on the NE, which may trigger the contraction of the acto-myosin network on the NE remnants.
evidence: Speculative mechanism proposed by authors.

claim: During cell migration, reduced membrane tension within lamellipodia led to local contraction of the acto-myosin network.
source: Similar mechanisms have been reported (Pontes et al., 2017); for example, during cell migration, reduced membrane tension within lamellipodia led to local contraction of the acto-myosin network (Gauthier et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on cited literature describing analogous mechanisms.

claim: In starfish oocytes, actin depolymerization beneath the nuclear envelope remnants facilitates the interaction of chromosomes with spindle microtubules.
source: For example, in starfish oocytes, actin depolymerization beneath the NE remnants facilitates the interaction of chromosomes with spindle MTs (Burdyniuk et al., 2018; Lénárt et al., 2005).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: In Xenopus embryos, spindle integrity relies on actin on the spindle and myosin-10 at spindle poles.
source: In Xenopus embryos, spindle integrity relies on actin on the spindle and myosin-10 at spindle poles (Woolner et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: In PtK2 cells, actin and non-muscle myosin on the mitotic spindle regulate the length of the spindle.
source: In PtK2 cells, actin and non-muscle myosin on the mitotic spindle regulate the length of the spindle (Sheykhani et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: In mouse oocytes, actin dynamics on the spindle promote robust kinetochore–MT interactions.
source: In mouse oocytes, actin dynamics on the spindle promote robust kinetochore–MT interactions (Mogessie and Schuh, 2017).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: Actin and myosin-II on the cell cortex are important for formation and correct orientation of the mitotic spindle.
source: Moreover, several studies suggest that actin and myosin-II on the cell cortex are important for formation and correct orientation of the mitotic spindle (Rosenblatt et al., 2004; Whitehead et al., 1996; Kunda and Baum, 2009).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: The actin cytoskeleton and non-muscle myosin appear to contribute to high-fidelity chromosome segregation through multiple mechanisms.
source: Thus, the actin cytoskeleton and non-muscle myosin appear to contribute to high-fidelity chromosome segregation through multiple mechanisms.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of current findings with cited literature.

claim: Chromosomes initially interact with the lateral side of spindle microtubules, and the consequent positioning of the chromosomes facilitates their bi-orientation.
source: For example, chromosomes initially interact with the lateral side of spindle MTs, and the consequent positioning of the chromosomes facilitates their bi-orientation (Magidson et al., 2011; Itoh et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: Bi-orientation causes chromosomes to move to the middle of the mitotic spindle.
source: Bi-orientation itself causes chromosomes to move to the middle of the mitotic spindle.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of mitotic processes.

claim: Chromosome movements to the middle of the spindle could occur prior to bi-orientation, facilitated by chromosome sliding along pre-existing spindle microtubules.
source: These movements could also occur prior to bi-orientation, facilitated by chromosome sliding along pre-existing spindle MTs (Kapoor et al., 2006; Barisic et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on cited literature.

claim: If chromosomes were located far away from the spindle poles, more time would be required to establish the initial chromosome–MT interaction.
source: If chromosomes were located far away from the spindle poles, more time would be required to establish the initial chromosome–MT interaction.
evidence: Based on logical reasoning about spatial relationships and interaction kinetics.

claim: If chromosomes were located behind a spindle pole, their interaction with microtubules from the other spindle pole would be significantly delayed.
source: Moreover, should chromosomes be located behind a spindle pole, that is opposite from the bulk of spindle and outside of the pole-to-pole region, their interaction with MTs from the other spindle pole would be significantly delayed.
evidence: Based on logical reasoning about spatial relationships and interaction kinetics.

claim: The convex hull in two and three dimensions is the minimal polygon and polyhedron, respectively, that wrap multiple objects.
source: The convex hull in two and three dimension (2D and 3D) is the minimal polygon and polyhedron, respectively, that wrap multiple objects (chromosomes in this case).
evidence: Definition of mathematical concept used in the study.

claim: The volume of the minimal polyhedron that wrapped chromosomes was defined as the chromosome scattering volume (CSV).
source: We determined the volume of this minimal polyhedron or shrunk balloon that wrapped chromosomes, and defined it as the chromosome scattering volume (CSV), which represents how widely chromosomes scatter in 3D space.
evidence: Definition of the measurement used in the study.

claim: U2OS cdk1-as cells were arrested in G2 with 1NM-PP1 and subsequently released by 1NM-PP1 washout to synchronously undergo mitosis.
source: The U2OS cdk1-as cells were arrested in G2 with 1NM-PP1, and subsequently released by 1NM-PP1 washout to synchronously undergo mitosis.
evidence: Description of experimental method.

claim: NEBD was identified by the release of the nuclear-localizing fluorescent reporter (GFP-LacI-NLS) into the cytoplasm.
source: NEBD was identified by the release of the nuclear-localizing fluorescent reporter (GFP-LacI-NLS) into the cytoplasm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
